Penny.title: $1 million or a penny doubled for 30 days?
Penny.desc:
Jordan takes $1,000,000 today. Riley takes one cent that doubles every day for 30 days. On day 20 the penny is worth just $5,242.88. It passes the million on day 28, and on day 30 it is worth $5,368,709.12. Half of it arrives on the last day. A thought experiment: no real investment doubles daily, but compounding has the same shape.

Every figure is calculated, with the assumptions shown on screen. Illustration only. Not financial advice.

WarVote.title: 49 to 50: the vote on ending the Iran war
WarVote.desc:
On 24 September 2026 the Senate voted 49 to 50 on a resolution directing an end to U.S. involvement in the Iran war. One senator did not vote. It was the 14th Senate vote on Iran war powers since the war began on 28 February; 13 have failed. The one that passed, in June (Senate 50-48, House 215-208), was a concurrent resolution that never goes to the president, and experts called it largely symbolic. In July, the House passed a new resolution 214-208; the Senate rejected it 47-49.

Sources: ABC News (24 Sep 2026), Al Jazeera (24 Jun and 23 Jul 2026), Carolina Political Review (15 Oct 2026).

Part of the series: The Iran war, in numbers. This video reports figures only and does not endorse any party or candidate.

WarBill.title: The Iran war bill: $320 per household so far
WarBill.desc:
By the Pentagon's own count, the Iran war cost the U.S. military $43.6 billion from 28 February to 3 September 2026: about $230 million a day, or about $320 per U.S. household. In June the White House requested $67.1 billion more for the Pentagon (about $500 per household). In July the House passed a budget plan with $73 billion for the Pentagon and national security, 216-214. The Congressional Budget Office estimates $2-3 billion for every further month. Figures overlap and are not additive.

Sources: Roll Call (18 Sep 2026), Aviation Week (24 Jun 2026), PBS NewsHour (22 Jul 2026), U.S. Census/FRED households (2025).

Part of the series: The Iran war, in numbers. This video reports figures only and does not endorse any party or candidate.

AfterVote.title: Gas prices after the midterms: the forecast
AfterVote.desc:
What the U.S. Energy Information Administration expects after 3 November. Brent oil closed at $72.48 before the war (27 Feb); EIA forecasts an average of $105 for October-December 2026. Regular gas was $2.98 before the war and $4.26 today (AAA, 21 Oct); EIA forecasts $3.56 for 2027. Diesel is $6.32 today, forecast about $4.50 in 2027, vs $3.76 before the war. Homes heating with oil are forecast to pay about 21% more this winter.

Sources: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook and Winter Fuels Outlook (6 Oct 2026), AAA (21 Oct 2026). Forecasts can change.

HumanCost.title: The cost of the Iran war no budget covers
HumanCost.desc:
The human cost of the 2026 Iran war, in numbers. The Pentagon reports 21 U.S. service members killed and 865 wounded (October 2026). In Iran, the rights group HRANA has counted 3,684 deaths, more than 1,700 of them civilians and at least 254 children. Lebanon's health ministry reports 4,383 killed; Israel, 72; Gulf states, around 50. Together, more than 8,000 people. Sources and dates differ.

Sources: Pentagon via The Washington Post (Oct 2026), HRANA, Lebanese Health Ministry, compiled in Wikipedia's Casualties of the 2026 Iran war.

Ep1.title: She saved for 10 years. He saved for 30. She ended up with more.
Ep1.desc:
Maya saves $200 a month for 10 years, then stops. Leo saves the same $200 a month for 30 years. Maya puts in a third as much, and still ends up with more: $280,968 against $243,994 at 65. This episode explains why, and what it means for you: how compounding works, what waiting really costs, why small amounts and low fees matter, what happens in a crash, the employer match, and how much you need each month to reach $1 million by 65.

Chapters
0:00 Two savers, one stops early
0:50 The penny puzzle
1:41 Deposits add, returns multiply
2:27 The most expensive habit: waiting
3:16 Small amounts, big numbers
3:56 The rate matters: the rule of 72 and fees
4:57 What if the market crashes?
5:46 Free money: the employer match
6:21 The million-dollar question
7:10 Three things to take away

Assumptions: a steady 7% a year, compounded monthly, before fees, tax and inflation, unless stated. The penny example is a thought experiment. Real returns vary, and markets fall as well as rise. Every figure is calculated, with the assumptions shown on screen. An illustration only, not financial advice.
